text: Bai Ganyo, having finally convinced himself that he had no chance of settling down at Irecheka's place, picked up his saddlebags, ignoring the landlord's exhortations to leave them at his house until he found a room, and set off, accompanied by his servant, for the Nàrodny Kavàrna — the café where Bulgarian students gather. It was already seven o'clock when he entered the café with his saddlebags in his hand and a cap on his head. Go, you won't recognize who he is and where he's from! To the left of the entrance, around a table, were sitting several Bulgarian students.

One of them saw the incoming compatriot and pushed the others: "Bulgarian, Bulgarian!" Everyone turned around at the moment when Bai Ganyo stopped a waiter carrying a tray of coffees, and, trying as much as possible to distort the Bulgarian words to make them understandable to the foreigner, asked in a loud voice: "Are there any Bulgarian boys here?" - and accompanied the question with a movement of the head and his free hand. A friendly laugh from the left side ended the waiter's bewilderment. Bai Ganyo turned around and recognized his black-eyed, black-haired, huddled compatriots.

"Oh! Good afternoon! Have you been here?" he shouted from the heart, put down his saddlebags and began to grab the students' hands. "What are you looking at me for? Don't be afraid, I'm Bulgarian... Make a place for me to sit down."
"What do they call you, sir?" one of the students asked curiously.
"Me? Why do you ask? Ganyo Balkanski. I brought some gun oil to your Prague - here it is in the saddlebags."
"Is that so?" cried one of the younger students in patriotic ecstasy. "Let us see it."
He had really only heard of rose oil.

"What are you going to do with it, butter is butter," replied Bai Ganyo, "it's not for you. Leave the butter alone, and tell me something else: where should I stay? I was just now at Bai Irecheka's..."
“Is that so?” the excited student shouted again.

— How "that"? Why shouldn't I go to him? I went — I thought, he'll show his humanity, he'll invite me to visit them. That faith! My apartment is cramped, oh my, I don't know what, oh my. He loved, oh my, the Bulgarians... Is that him! When there's gossip, and bye Ganyo knows how to love. — Is that how you greet a Bulgarian? A Bulgarian!... I won't lie to you, feed me the man. And what kind of food — oh my, stuff it!... Where are the Bulgarians more hospitable; the Bulgarian, if he has a room, will still invite you...

Some of the students began to wonder where Bai Ganyo was going and waited every minute for him to reveal his cards. Only the excited student reacted sympathetically to his words and clearly shared his indignation at the inhospitality of the foreigners.
"Indeed, our Bulgarians are very hospitable," he confirmed with the utmost confidence, "the locals don't want to know you. We're soaking up the coffee here..."

The student who said these words was very advanced in civilization, but for some reason he did not enjoy a special reputation among his comrades; it seems that some sins lay on his soul; they said, by the way, that he was very fond of "slandering." No wonder! This desolate sin - stinginess - by contagion of the surrounding home environment takes root almost from childhood; it dries up the soul of the young man, turning him into the coldest egoist: nothing tender, nothing noble remains in him. Material interest governs all the actions of the stingy man and determines his relations to those around him: no moral impulse precedes, no remorse follows his actions, aimed without analysis of the means at obtaining benefits. Even when these actions bring disaster or disgrace to someone, then instead of remorse the selfish-stingy feels satisfaction, as if the loss of others is his gain, the misfortune of others is his happiness. One thing would disturb our young selfish - if someone outsmarted him. While in other nations the word "cunning" is synonymous with cunning, treacherous and attached to a person, it would lower him in the opinion of society, in our country the epithet cunning is adorned as with the most honorable decoration: "Bray! A cunning boy came out, may his father live, he deceived us all! We could not deceive him! Ashkolsun. Bravo!"

No actions or relationships made sense to Bodkova—that was his name—if they did not result in something naughty, some gossip. (Are there words in European languages ​​that correspond to these, in this sense?) If he visited the families there, he did so not out of sociability, out of a desire to get acquainted with the way of life in more civilized circles; the intellectual and moral interests of this society not only did not occupy him, but were also a burden to him—they seemed to be boring intervals, unbearable pauses that separated him from the purpose of his visits—from the naughty: now some treat, now some walk at their expense. He could not imagine getting to know women without ulterior motives. He kept a whole list of girls—whose dowries were how much; he was not interested in anything else in this respect. Interest also determined his relations with his comrades. Flattery, slander, intrigues and denunciations were the tools of his advantage. Even such things as national and tribal sympathies and antipathies served him only to extract personal benefit. More than once he rummaged in the pockets of various Slavic committees, sometimes as a "Batak", sometimes as an "emigrant". But Aslanov is a master at these things.

Such was the exalted student who supported Bai Ganya in his opinion about the hospitality of foreigners. "Yes, we're hanging around here in the cafes, no one invites us to visit," he repeated to please Bai Ganya.

"And you want to be left to rot?" said a bilious-looking student, who had evidently long harbored a hatred for the young egoist. "Do you want to be carried in your arms? Why? Because you haven't even crossed the threshold of their house yet, you will first hook the maid who meets you in the hallway! Because in their company you are either silent as an oak tree, or you open your mouth only to babble vulgarities and nonsense? Because you will praise them to the heavens to their faces, and slander them behind their backs? Because you will throw dust in their eyes and recommend yourself as the son of a millionaire manufacturer or shipowner, when your father has two wheels for a braid or two pierced crows - just so that you can call the parents and carry off their daughter? Why will they receive you with open arms? Who are you? What kind of person are you to them? In whose eyes are you showing off your hospitality? And what is this vaunted hospitality of yours! — Is it that the Bulgarian will spread you a greasy bed and wrap you in questionable clothing? Ah, for God's sake, stop these savage boasts! Isn't it time we opened our eyes?
"What are you so angry about? Did you find the time to fight now," one of the students said, "when we have a guest coming?"

— Let the man show himself, he doesn't want money? — Uncle Ganyo calmed him down with this typical argument: "He wants Paris!" He can say whatever he wants, do whatever he wants, as long as he doesn't want money, as long as he doesn't touch our pockets, our interests. He can lie, he doesn't want money!

But after this chance incident, a friendly conversation could no longer be maintained. The company quieted down and one after another began to disperse. Of the Bulgarians, only Bai Ganyo and the excited student remained, who did not want to miss the opportunity to derive some benefit from his chance meeting with the Bulgarian rose oil merchant. — The saucepan rolled over because it found its lid.

Not an hour had passed before the student had managed to scold his comrades in front of Bai Ganya so much that he had made him shout with all his heart: "Ashkolsun kyopoolar!" After another hour, Bai Ganya was already in the student's room, who was quite adept at exploiting to his advantage the arrival of a guest whom he had recommended to his landlords as a relative, a millionaire who "has a number of rose oil factories." He had managed to borrow ten guilders from the landlady—to whom he had not paid the rent for the room for a long time. While in one room the student was extolling Bai Ganya's wealth, in the next room Bai Ganya had already taken off his apron and was searching for something in it with great care, grumbling under his breath: "That empty bastard has got it up again." Bai Ganya's concept of cleanliness was not very highly developed. "Is there a living person without a bastard?" — say the old people in our country and, reassured by this axiom, they do not hinder the reproduction of animals too diligently. And why would they deprive themselves of such a pleasure: a sunny day, why is that sun good for him if he cannot go out on the veranda, stretch out on the mat, sneeze two or three times from its dust, so that his grandmother can come, so that he can put his head on her knee, so that she can dig her bony fingers with mourning nails into his hair and, as if she needed rice, start hammering! — this way, hammering! — that way, when the animals get scared, when they slide on the head, then a pleasant tickle, when the grandmother sings, and that sun of yours is a Balkan sunny day! Idyllic...

Bai Ganyo, having finished his entomological research, put on his clothes and, without knocking, entered the next room, but immediately shouted: "Excuse me!" - and there was reason for it: he found the student and the landlady's daughter in a very tender vis a vis - they had embraced each other, as befits two young hearts in love. The girl, embarrassed, ran into the other room.
"Why are you coming in like that? You're embarrassing the girl," the student said with an ironic wink.
"You've hit the nail on the head!" whispered Bai Ganyo mysteriously, his eyes shining like a monastery cat's. "She's shiny, damn it! Is she a maid?"
"What a servant! The landlady's daughter!"

"Is that so? Here you can't tell who's a servant and who's a mistress, they're all shiny, all neatly dressed. One comes up to you, smiling so smugly, you think she's a servant, you pick on her, you get in trouble; another comes up to you, pretty, humble, you think she's the mistress, you stand up to her, invite her to sit down, she's embarrassed—oh my!—you talk to her politely, and then you see her cleaning your boots!"

From the student's stories, accompanied by various gestures with which he embellished and gave more force and meaning to his words, Bai Ganyo learned that for several months, under the guise of pure love, the young man had been attacking the daughter of his widowed landlady with irresistible insistence.

"And she, the divan," the narrator explains, "hopes that I will take her as my wife! Let her hope and let her feed me well, let her sew me shirts. If she were a rich woman, I understand why someone would take her, but she's a scoundrel like me. She's wrapped around me because she thinks I'm rich. If she knew what I was like, would she want to? These people here are terrible speculators! But I know how to spin them, too?" And he told her at length how he spins them...
"Ashkolsun!" shouted Bai Ganyo, his eyes watery, delighted with his young interlocutor.

"Wait, is that all? If that's it, it's not! There's another one, another one, I've got my eye on her, but who knows! I can't even wrap my head around it - there's something to hit. Rich! I've been invited to their house tomorrow, they're taking me for a walk to a village."
"And when will you take me to the factories?" asked the practical Mr. Gagno.

"Easy job, another day. You stay here tomorrow, hang around them, when they see you don't know the language, they won't let you go to the inn, they'll invite you to their house and you'll eat a lot of crap."

And indeed, the next morning the student went to visit, and Bai Ganyo stayed in the apartment with only the landlords. As usual, that day he got up very early, woke up and sent his friend away, and waited another hour until the landlady woke up. This waiting was very hard for him, he felt some great need, like any person, so he forgot to ask the student where that thing was and — willy-nilly — he had to wait for the housekeepers to get up and — shame on me — ask them. It's very bad when you don't know a foreign language, they can't understand you about the simplest things, you always have to tell them with your hands, with your fingers, show them... And does everything show itself? Bai Ganyo knew languages, he could speak Turkish to you like a Turk, he understood Vlach, Serbian, Russian chat-pat, but the Germans and Czechs didn't understand any of these languages. It can't be said that Bai Ganyo didn't know German at all, he knew a word or two.

In the next room the housekeepers got up and were moving about. Bai Ganyo looked through the keyhole, not out of any indecent curiosity, but to see if they were already dressed, and carefully, with bated breath, as he familiarized himself with their attire, he composed in his mind a phrase in German that would correspond to ours: "Where is that for big work?" — and finally, from the literal translation, he combined the phrase: "Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit?" — Knock! knock! knock!
“Prosim!” two female voices called from the next room.
Bai Ganyo opened the door, said a "forgive me" and shyly said: "Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit?" and moved his fingers to emphasize the question.
"What, pàn?" the girl asked in bewilderment, trying to examine the appearance of the millionaire recommended by her lover.
"Fur gross Arbeit?" repeated Bai Gagno, even more confused, and again moved his fingers and head, but he noticed that they did not understand him.
They understood him, but not as they should have; the women thought he was telling them that he had come to do great things, a great trade in rose oil.

"Oh, the devil!" thought Bai Ganya. "What should I do now?" And so that at least his daughter would not witness his predicament, he called his mother into his room with his hand, closed the door, and after repeating the question in German, this time supplemented it with a desperate facial expression that made the lady run away, choking with restrained laughter, into the other room. The maid appeared and satisfied Bai Ganya's curiosity. A trio of continuous female laughter shook the walls.
The aroma coming out of the open kitchen door into the hallway whetted Uncle Ganya's appetite, and out of curiosity he peeked in to see what they were cooking. The landlady and the maid were there.

— Was ist das? — asked Bai Gagno in a condescending tone, not so much out of a desire to get acquainted with the culinary art of the Czechs as to show that he had been around Europe and knew these things, and could even speak German. — Soup, right? You're cooking soup? I know. Ich versten supa!

And Bai Ganyo, with a mixture of German, Bulgarian and distorted Bulgarian, aided by impressive gestures, gave the landlady to understand that he would not refuse to taste the taste of their cuisine. Seeing that the women showed a greater inclination to explain themselves in Czech, Bai Ganyo turned to "Czech" and supported his indulgent desire with the words: "I want to eat it," interpreting these words by repeatedly touching his fingers to his open mouth, and then, pointing to his three fingers, he pushed his chest with his index finger, pushed the same finger to the landlady's chest and pointed a third time into space, as if pointing to the landlady's invisible daughter, i.e. "to eat it, you three!" It was also important for Bai Ganyo to know what time he would have lunch, because he was going to go for a walk, so as not to miss lunch, and then "give me money to eat, while there is no money, you bastard", and so he took out his huge watch and, holding it in front of the landlady's nose, made her show him with her finger the hands when he would "have lunch". When he was sure that everything was in order, Bai Ganyo went into his room, stuffed the muskets into his belt and went out into the street to take a walk, so that he would both take a walk and maybe run into a customer for rose oil.

Look, Ganyo, the streets intersect a lot, you can get lost, you can get lost, and like a practical man, he looked around to see some sign by which he could recognize the house, and saw on the opposite side, on a back wall, an inscription in large letters; he took out his notebook, squinted at the vase, wrote an exact copy of the inscription and, completely confident that he had in his hands the most accurate address of his apartment, he ventured through the narrow streets of old Prague, and he looked here, he looked there, he saw a customer here, he saw a customer there, he got carried away and let him get carried away, but he lost his way. What now? What if he set out to look for his house, that he got lost even more through the Jewish streets, and an hour passed, two hours passed, he got stuck in some house - there was no way out, he went in another direction, he walked, walked and jumped out onto the banks of the Vltava. "Come on, devil, what now?" Well, leave the rest, but it's time for lunch, it came and went. That old man Ganyo, leaning on his haunches, walking, walking, he's a puddle of water, panting, he doesn't look like anything. The people he met, especially the police, looked at him suspiciously: this embarrassed him even more. "Come on, the devil, what now?" He was hungry, with a revolution in his stomach, but what the hell would he throw his money away for when he's invited to lunch?

But, you will say, why is Uncle Ganyo wandering around the streets when the address is in his pocket? Well, that's the point! Uncle Ganyo is not a simpleton, you think, if he didn't think to take out his notebook, stop this and that guy on the street and, pointing to the written address, ask him with his fingers "where to?" He knows these things, he stops both men and women, but a strange thing - whoever he stops to ask, when he points out the written address, they will either look at him in amazement and laugh, or turn away from him with indignation. One lady, probably some nervous old maid, when she showed her the address, so jumped at him that Uncle Ganyo lost his courage. "Come on, the devil, either I'm crazy, or all of Prague has gone crazy," he thinks to himself and cannot help but be amazed at the effect that his written address produces; He is both thinking and looking around, and at one point—isn't that happiness?—he sees the Nàrodny Kavàrna, the café where Bulgarian students gather, looming before him. Uncle Ganyo enters and finds the angry student.
"Good afternoon! Tell me, your grace, am I crazy, are the people here crazy?" asks Bai Ganyo, panting, with wet hair stuck to his forehead.
The student looked at him questioningly. Bai Ganyo told him how he had gotten lost, how he had asked about his house by address, and what they had told him.
The student, knowing that the Czechs, rude and fanatical only towards the Germans, are otherwise quite polite, cannot help but wonder how they could not do anything for Uncle Ganya.
"Read, please, what's written here!" and Uncle Ganyo handed over the notebook.
The student read it: at first he frowned, but then he snorted!...
“Did you show this address to any lady?” he asked through laughter.
"Why? I showed it to you! Well?"
"Well? Do you know what's written here?"
"What?"
— It says "...Zde je zapovedeno..." "It is forbidden here to..." You copied it from a wall somewhere.
"There's a has! Look! T... t... t! Are you telling the truth? Look!" said Uncle Ganyo, clicked his tongue a little, and he started laughing too.

The student didn't know Bodkova's apartment, they didn't go to each other's, and so he advised Bai Ganya to wait, and some Bulgarian would come and show him the house. It's easy to say "wait," but Bai Ganya's stomach, let's see if it's of the same opinion! And that he wasn't of the same opinion, he demonstratively proved with an endless gurgling.
“Aren't you hungry?” the student asked him, hearing the revolutionary signals.

"Who, me?" "I'm not," lied Bai Ganyo, because if he told the truth, the man would show him the inn, and he didn't want to admit ("How can I tell such a stubborn kid!") that a delicious meal was waiting for him at the landlady's.

A conversation between Bai Ganyo and the "stubborn kid" could not be established. From the first meeting and instinctively, they somehow realized that they were not meant for each other, because according to the Bulgarian proverb (oh, what exquisite proverbs the Bulgarian genius created!) "cucumber donkeys can be smelled for nine miles". One came from Bulgaria, the other lived in Europe, they would still have something to talk about, because there must be some difference between the West and our homeland. Besides, Bai Ganyo did not notice this difference, and how will he notice it! Wherever he goes, he brings with him his own atmosphere, his own customs and habits, looks for a place to live according to his own tastes, meets all his own people, to whom he is accustomed and in whom, of course, he sees nothing new: if he goes to Vienna, he will stop at the "London" hotel, it is just as stuffy there, it smells just as much of cooking and hydrogen sulfide as at home; he meets the same Turks, Armenians, Serbs, and Arnauts that he is accustomed to meeting every day; he will not go to the Habsburg Café because he is afraid of being robbed, but will go back to the Greek café, which is just as unclean and suffocated by eternal smoke as our cafés. If he goes to trade, he will go to the Bulgarian merchants, and through them he does not even realize that he is coming into contact with Europeans. And that it is precisely outside this limited sphere that European life begins, he does not know and does not even seem to want to know. The upbringing, the moral peace of the European, his home environment - the fruit of centuries-old tradition and the gradual perfection of intellectual movement - the social struggles and the way they are conducted, the museums, libraries, philanthropic institutions, the fine arts, the thousands of manifestations of progress do not burden the attention of Bai Ganya.

"Because my father always listened to operas," says Bai Gagno, and, charmed by this principle of fossilization and ultra-retrogradism, he is not too much frightened by the "new fashion," i.e., by civilization. But for all this, Bai Gagno does not have the valor of the Chinese - to fence himself off with a wall against the invasion of civilization - and for all that he is inspired by the principle "my father did not do this and I will not do it," but you see that you have put on a clean shirt, put on gloves, and when they see him, he puts on a tailcoat, gets angry, laughs, but puts on the tailcoat. You hear him say "pardon," talk about "constentuity," brag to himself that he likes "soup," when in fact he would prefer a hot soup to all European dishes.
"Ah, here comes a Bulgarian, he knows Bodkova's apartment," said the "recalcitrant kid"...

"Come on, take me home," said Bai Ganya to the little Bulgarian in a tone that should disappear in our relations with lazy servants; but the words "politeness," "politeness" are newly stolen from the Russian language, "delicacy" was borrowed from the French, and in our country the most suitable term for these concepts is the word "drooling." Those soft, gentle, cordial addresses that characterize the relations of civilized people and that make life kinder, more pleasant—are incomprehensible to Bai Ganya; he speaks as God has given him: "Come on, hey, listen, take me home." And what does he mean: "Please, be so kind, be so kind," what are these droolings!...

The Bulgarian took Bai Ganya to the gate of his quarters and returned. Bai Ganya looked at the unfortunate inscription on the wall he came across, shook his head at him, clicked his tongue and entered the house. He didn't meet anyone in the corridor, so he peeked into the kitchen - the fire was already out there, the dishes were cleaned and put away. "Oh, you idiot, I missed the chatterbox," scolded Bai Ganya, went into his room, crouched over his saddlebags, took the muskals out of his belt, stuffed them inside, pulled out the buttered cheese, cut himself a dry loaf of bread and began to smother the revolution, munching so appetizingly that even the laziest Swiss cow would envy him. To irritate his lymphatic organs, tired of unproductive work, he swallowed a chewed Arnaut pepper, which made him weep and accompanied his slurping with a sniff. The maid, who was walking in the next room, hearing the strange sounds with which Bai Gagno accompanied his breakfast, opened the door and peered into the room: Bai Gagno shyly covered the saddlebags with his back, turned his tear-stained and sweaty face, said: "Excuse me!", blew his nose energetically and chased the maid away, that is, he did not tell her to leave, but she hurried to run away, thinking that the millionaire might have received some sad news.

Bodkov did not return in the evening. Towards evening the landlady came home; a fire was lit in the kitchen again and they began to cook dinner. Bai Ganyo considered himself familiar, "and after all, what are you going to do with women?" he said, and without any preface he entered the kitchen and explained more with mimicry than with words that he had gotten lost in the streets and missed lunch, but it didn't matter - he had to have lunch, he would make up for it with dinner. Bai Ganyo also understood the art of cooking, and not only did he understand, but any violation of this craft outraged him. For example, he saw that the landlady was preparing to put a fresh fish in the boiling water, and he got up with all his energy, grabbed the landlady's hand, pulled the fish out with his other hand and made a sign with his hand and head, which he wanted to say: "Stop, don't mess around, just watch how the fish is being cooked!" "Salt"! Bai Ganyo commanded. They give him salt, he rolls up his sleeves to the elbows of his hairy arms, reaches into the salt shaker with his not-so-delicate fingers and begins to salt and rub the already salted fish inside and out. "Red pepper!" - but where will these sofas have red pepper! "Black pepper" - orders Bai Ganya, grabs the pepper and rubs it on the fish. "Grill!" - trumpets the triumphant chef, but here they could not understand him, with all his gestures, and he himself glanced around and could not notice the grill; but is this an obstacle for Bai Ganya? He is not the same as yesterday! Taking the tongs, he poured all the fire in front of the opening of the oven, let the other dishes rest (it was a good thing that they were already ready), spread the tongs, put the fish on them and said to put it in the oven, but the door is narrow, the fish got stuck, slipped and - splat! — into the fire. “Oh!” — cried the landlady. “Nothing, nothing!” — Bai Ganya reassured her, grabbed the fish, blew off the stuck coals and ashes and put it back on the grill. Smoke and the smell of fish filled the entire kitchen. The landlady — in despair, Bai Ganya shine, he is now in his own sphere; he is both roasting the fish and blowing, and sniffing, irritated by the appetizing smoke, and at the same time ordering with his free hand, which was worn from turning the fish, to set the table so that his feast would not get cold: “Isn’t fresh fish hot — throw it!” The fish, roasted, with its tail and head covered in ashes, was placed on a plate and under Bai Ganya’s kind command: “Quick! Quick! While it is hot, give me lemon and wine, without wine it doesn’t cost a penny!” — they sat down around the table, sending the maid to run for lemon and wine. What will they do! The millionaire will not change his habits for their pleasure! The landlady reached out to cut the fish. "Please, please, please! Saken!" cried Bai Ganyo and took her hand, then turned the fish on its back, pressed it right there with her two fingers and it split into two halves. Well, go, don't celebrate! The maid brought a lemon, Bai Ganyo cut it, grabbed half with a whole handful and squeezed it over the plate with such diligence that even the fleshy parts of the lemon fell over the fish. What do you think, does Bai Ganyo have no appetite? I don't think as much lemon juice flowed into the plate as Bai Ganyo swallowed saliva. And they brought wine. The dinner began.

Carlsbad and I don't know what kind of medicine the Aesculapius recommends for those suffering from catarrh in the stomach. Let them take these sufferers by the ear and put them on the table in front of Mr. Ganya, and let their stomachs be spoiled more than the streets of Yuchbunar... you'll see what effect the spectacle will have on them!... Mr. Ganya eats, oh my, he's not kidding, he eats, and his ears pop! All the organs of his body are in motion, and his teeth, tongue and nose in the first place. Here one realizes the pallor and poverty of language! With what words, with what interjections, with what punctuation marks, finally with what musical notes it is possible to depict these smacking, grunting, sniffing, rattling, clicking, sucking, which pour out like hail from Mr. Ganya!... Blessed are the housewives! Not every Czech woman will have the happiness to enjoy such a spectacle.

They finally ate. They went into the reception room. Bai Ganyo, red as a peony, was sucking his mustache, belching with his fist, and muttering "pardon." They settled down on the chairs. Bai Ganyo rolled a cigarette, greased by his fingers, and began to suck and blow clouds of smoke through his mustache. Isn't this the most opportune moment for pleasure: for music, for songs, for love? The girl caught the millionaire's mood and asked him if he liked music. Who? Bai Ganyo? Well, if Bai Ganyo doesn't like music, who else will? Who else could instill in the gypsies, that is, the musicians, such respect for themselves as Bai Ganyo? Just by blinking an eye, look what happens to these gypsies! Fire! Fire! Turn on that violin of yours, make that clarinet scream!
Your strength is a poplar,
on my heart like two wheels.
It's on your dress
Burn my liver...

— Sus 6e, cops! I don't want love affairs! He's playing on my brandy! — shouted Bai Ganyo to them and banged his glass on the table. They started "Karan-klangfilcheto", Bai Ganyo banged his glass, stopped. They started "Ne shte mi niy bostozh" — banged his glass again. Turned to "Zelen leafets". "Ha, did you see now! E-e-e-e-h! Gel kefim, gel!"... — and slammed the bottle into the ground or into the window... Well, who is the master of these things? And was it once, was it twice? But how will these women know who Bai Ganyo is! Even if you tell them how many windows you've broken with music, they won't understand you!...

"I love music!" said Bai Ganyo condescendingly. "I love music!" he repeated and shook his head, which in his opinion expressed the sad necessity of listening to the miserable twang of a piano for the sake of women. "What do you understand by a srvirnya, by mohabet?" thought Bai Ganyo.

The girl opened the piano and began some endless pieces from "Prodana nevesta" by Smetana. The sounds that bring every Czech soul to ecstasy poured out from under her fingers. Her mother, who was probably hearing these pieces for the thousandth and first time, was lost in bliss, and in her gaze, turned to Bai Ganya, national pride and self-satisfaction shone; she kept her head in time with the tempo of the piece, now adagio, now allegro, as if she were punctuating the notes of the fioritures with her nose. From time to time she would make signs to Bai Ganya with her eyes, warning him of the arrival of some favorite moment in the play, and the millionaire would answer: "Be careful, your grace, don't look at me, I've heard them so many times!..." And to back up this sign in action, he got up from his chair at the very moment when the landlady expected to enjoy the effect that Smetana would produce on Bai Ganya, and quickly, with a plan in his head, went to his room, took the open sample bottle from his saddlebags and returned to the reception room, winked at his mother: "Look what will produce an effect," tiptoed over to the girl, who was engrossed in the music, and—what a terrible devil that Bai Ganya was!—opened the bottle with the rose oil and gently pushed it under the girl's nose. She, feeling the breath of Bai Ganyo's sweaty hand, smelling of fish, turned away in disgust and, carried away by the music, at first looked at him with a frown, but immediately came to her senses that the millionaire was standing in front of her, grinning at her, and asking her: "Is your Smetana resting, or the one where you smelled it, huh?" - and tucked the muskala into her belt... The girl stopped playing. Bai Ganyo began... (What did you say? - I couldn't understand you!)... He began to play carelessly with one finger, without sitting down on the chair: "As long as I give these people to understand that we understand a little bit of these scoundrels too." A relative of Bai Ganyo's had a hand-held harmonica with keys that now and then, when he felt like it, Bai Ganyo would break his fingers to make up a song. Now he began a startled pizzicato, which in his opinion represented the song: "She stole it," this grandmother, sla-slanin-kaa, slaninka, this grandmother stole the slaninka... which "Slaninka" was entirely stolen from the Czech "Slaninka."
— Pan is playing "Slaninku", mom! — the girl announced her discovery.
— "Slaninka" sir — said Bai Ganyo, — how do you know it?

Delighted by the success, Bai Ganyo sat down on the chair to play, now with good reason, something more serious. And what could be more serious than "The Night is Terrible"? Bai Ganyo began to play, but he was left dissatisfied with the performance. And quite naturally! "The Night is Terrible" was not created for piano; the sounds intersect: you press the key on "uh-a-a-sna-a!" and the voice intersects; the harmonica is another thing! When you put your finger on "... zh-a-a-sna-a..." - press his old mother! Let it rumble for half an hour, press, twist in waves, until you feel like it! And with the piano - bang, bang, wind! Uncle Ganyo saw that the effect produced by "The Bacon" would weaken, he thought, thought, and decided: "Well, wait, I'll sing "A Terrible Night" to these women!..." He thought for a moment, wanted to get into a sad mood, in the spirit of the mournful song, sighed once deeply, put his right hand to his ear, dozed with his eyes as if wide open!...

"Grandissimo Maestro Verdi! You have no, you cannot have enemies! But if, as you wish, some freak should appear, it will be Satan himself. God is great, Esimio Maestro! — and all the arrows of the evil spirit are powerless against you! Only one... only one means can the evil one use and the whole musical world will be covered in mourning... We will pray to Him, pray to you, Divine Maestro, to the almighty creator, not to allow Satan to lead you into the salon, in which Bai Gagno sings "The Night is Terrible"... And when your most delicate hearing is disturbed by the wild, inhuman sounds incomprehensible to you, may the Evil Spirit reveal to you the terrible truth with his satanic laughter: Ha! ha! ha! Verdi! This is a song from your divine "La Traviata"! Ha! ha! ha! ha-a!!..."
"It's late, gentlemen," said the shy Ilcho, looking at his watch, "midnight! Let's go, and another time, God willing, we'll talk about Uncle Ganya."

— Well, Ilcho, tell me, why do you hate Bulgarian songs so much? — said the little girl Dravichka on her way out. — Who? Should I hate them? I'm sorry, little dove, that you misunderstood me. I am capable of admiring, of forgetting, of being carried away to the point of ecstasy by our beautiful melancholic folk songs, but by Bulgarian songs, and not by those disgusting parodies of foreign vulgar songs that the Baiganiovites transmit to us, distorted beyond recognition through those gypsy forschlags and throat-clearing with drunken trills and flourishes... We have songs, but we have no singers. I am ready to embrace my enemy if he sings me the song "Bogdan, may God kill you" or "Hold it up, Velo girl, white sleeves" properly and to look askance at my friend when I see him admiring "Green Leaf", "The Carnation" and other such gypsy charms...
